Each round, a set of dice are rolled in the middle of the table, determining which kind of road and railway routes are available to all players. You have to draw these routes on your erasable boards to create transport lines and connect your exits, trying to optimize the available symbols better than your opponents. The more exits you connect, the more points you score at the end of the game, but you lose points for each incomplete route, so plan carefully! Will you press your luck and try to stretch your transportation network to the next exit, or will you play it safe and start a new, simpler to manage route? Railroad Ink comes in two versions, each one including two expansions with additional dice sets that add new special rules to your games. The Deep Blue Edition includes the Rivers and Lakes expansions. Increase the difficulty by adding the River route into the mix, or use the Lakes to connect your networks by ferry. These special rules can spice up things and make each game play and feel different. Each box allows you to play from 1 to 6 players, and if you combine more boxes, you can play with up to 12 players (or more). The only limit to the number of players is the number of boards you have! Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Each player draws route networks. The more Exits you connect to the same Network, the more points it will be worth. Bonus points can be earned for your Longest Railway, your Longest Highway, and by drawing on the Central Spaces of your Board. Contents 1 Base Game 1.1 Drawing routes 1.1.1 Route dice faces 1.2 Special Routes 1.3 End of the round 1.4 Score 1.4.1 Networks 1.4.2 Longest Highway 1.4.3 Longest Railway 1.4.4 Central spaces 1.4.5 Error 1.4.6 Expansion points 1.4.7 Total 2 Variants 2.1 Deep Blue Edition: River Dice 2.1.1 River dice faces 2.1.2 Changing rules 2.1.3 River score 2.2 Deep Blue Edition: Lake Dice 2.2.1 Lake dices face 2.2.2 Changing rules 2.2.3 Lake score 2.3 Blazing Red Edition: Meteor Dice 2.3.1 Meteor dices face 2.3.2 Changing rules 2.3.3 Meteor score 2.4 Blazing Red Edition: Lava Dice 2.4.1 Lava dices face 2.4.2 Changing rules 2.4.3 Lava score Base Game At the beginning of each round, the Route dice are rolled once. The results of the roll will determine which Routes all players must draw that round. After the roll, all players play simultaneously, drawing the Routes rolled on their own boards. The game ends at the end of the 7th round (6th round with expansions). Drawing routes Each Route you draw must be connected by at least one side to either one of the Exits or a preexisting Route. You must draw all 4 Routes (only once) shown on the dice each round, if possible. You can’t draw Routes in a way that directly connects Railways to Highways or vice versa (you need a Station to do that). You can freely rotate and/or reverse the pattern you see on the die. Route dice faces 3 dice have: Curved Railway T-junction Railway Straight Railway Curved Highway T-junction Highway Straight Highway 1 die has: 2 × Overpass (Straight Railway + Straight Highway, they are not connected) 2 × Straight Station (Railway and Highway are connected) 2 × Curved Station (Railway and Highway are connected) Special Routes Each player can also use 6 Special Routes, displayed at the top part of the boards Each special route can be used only once per player. You may draw a Special Route 1 per round , in addition to the Routes shown on the Route dice. You can only use up to 3 Special Routes during the entire game . End of the round The number of the round is added in each spaces where a route has been drawn. You can never erase the Routes you drew in a previous round. Score Networks For each networks, count the number of exits connected to it. Will you press your luck and try to stretch your transportation network to the next exit, or will you play it safe and start a new, simpler to manage route?

[Rating: 1/10] Solitaire. No arc. No substantial decisions.   At least the game is elegant, compare to other roll and writes, and it is fast.

[Rating: 1/10] [b]Route drawing as clerical exercise.[/b] Roll the dice, fit the roads and rails, connect exits, avoid dead ends. There is some spatial foresight in preserving future connections, but the dice dictate the vocabulary of every turn and the puzzle never grows beyond arranging whatever geometry happens to arrive. Neat, compact, and almost completely devoid of agency

[Rating: 2/10] Probably more interesting than some 'roll and write' games that I've played, but that isn't saying much; I'm a bit mystified why people would want to play a game like this multiplayer, given the experience is essentially the same as a solo game - I guess just in case they get the highest score and can say they won?

[Rating: 2/10] Blisteringly simple roll and write game. Normally not to my tastes, but I'd be lying if I said I didn't enjoy the entry-level "risk management" and luck pushing/mitigation involved. Innocuous, but amusing enough.

[Rating: 2.9/10] Interesting concept, but I don't think it's a great game and from a production standpoint it's not too high for me.

[Rating: 3/10] Having just enjoyed 30 Rails my expectations were already high for Railroad Ink. Unfortunately I found Railroad Ink very dull in comparison. Railroad Ink is a much more sandboxy game than 30 Rails. In 30 Rails you have a few specific routes you need to make. Here you score your networks in total. The extra freedom is more boring in my opinion. Additionally the track options are more interesting in 30 Rails than the two track types here. Overall I just found Railroad Ink to be much, much blander

[Rating: 3/10] Kurzrezension: "Railroad Ink" ist ein weiterer Vertreter der 'Roll and Write' Spiele.  Spielablauf: Pro Runde werden sechs Würfel geworfen, auf denen Straßen und Bahnlinien aufgedruckt sind. Alle Spieler müssen jetzt alle Würfelsymbole auf ihren eigenen Spielfeldern einzeichnen. Punkte gibt es am Ende für lange Strecken und verbundenen Ausgänge. Das Spiel endet, sobald alle Felder mit Symbolen ausgefüllt sind.  Meinung: "Railroad Ink" fand ich einfach nur schlecht. Der Zufall der Würfel ist gar nicht mal so groß, da jeder Spieler damit klarkommen muss. Aber bei diesem Spiel kam bei mir überhau

[Rating: 3/10] I didn't really care for the multiple different types of roads in this one. Avenue is very similar, but does in a much more simple way.

[Rating: 3/10] Just didn't click.  Thematically or mechanically, nothing grabbed us.  Not for me.

[Rating: 3/10] [2021]  Woof.  Try to plan a seven turn strategy with linear probabilities and no mitigation (no rerolls, changing faces, skipping dice, etc).  Roll 'em and fit 'em in, have fun storming the castle.  Far far far inferior to "Welcome To".

[Rating: 3/10] We've moved beyond this in roll-and-write games.  There are so many options that you can pick of good roll-and-write games that something as boring as this has no reason to exist in my collection.  The gameplay is kind of basic, and I find the entire thing to be somewhat annoying as the board starts to look really sloppy.  I'm not much of an artist, so it's partially on me, but drawing all this just gets so messy as the game goes on.
